newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Tanks move on to Tirana streets as unrest mounts.
newsitem.headline: Tanks move on to Tirana streets as unrest mounts.

text.p: Tanks moved onto the streets of Tirana late on Thursday night in an attempt to stem virtual anarchy gripping Albania.
At least two tanks could be seen deploying in the Albanian capital on the main Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation where key government buildings and the university are located.
Earlier, opposition political party leaders said Albanian President Sali Berisha had told them he was going to send in the tanks "to protect the main state institutions".

Their arrival coincided with mounting lawlessness in Albania, where rebels have raided army barracks and looted weapons, usually while demoralised soldiers have looked on without attempting to stop them.

The crackle of small arms fire interspersed with tracer rounds as insurgents discharged their weapons into the air, could be heard in Tirana against a backdrop of the roar of tank engines, but the level of firing appeared to diminish as the tanks patrolled up and down the main streets.
Albania's chaotic revolt, which began in the south where people have lost their savings in collapsed pyramid investment schemes, has spread to the north of the country in the past 48 hours.
Tirana itself has also seen growing unrest, with citizens looting a warehouse of 650 tonnes of flour on Thursday and raiding security force depots in search of guns,

As pressure mounted on Berisha from the rebels who want him to resign before they will consider handing back the arms they have stolen, two of his children fled to Italy by ferry with two armed bodyguards.

Albania's government called for foreign military intervention to halt the disorder, but German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the crisis was essentially an internal matter and it was not clear what foreign troops would do there.
As the unrest increased, Western governments began evacuating their nationals.

The United States sent four Chinook military helicopters into Tirana to pull out its citizens. About 50 Americans, most of them children, had already been ferried out of the country to U.S. ships standing offshore, the State Department said.
Italy used helicopters to rescue 400 foreign nationals and ferried them to Italian warships in the Adriatic. The evacuees were 330 Italians and 70 other foreigners.

Britain organised a pullout of 100 foreign nationals in a convoy of vehicles from Tirana to the port of Durres. The Foreign Office said 65 Britons, 52 people of other nationalities, 11 Commonwealth citizens and three from Ireland had arrived at the port ready for evacuation to Italy.

In the clearest sign yet that Berisha and the newly-formed coalition government were no longer in control, all political parties urged NATO's European members to use their military to end the turmoil.

All political forces in Albania agreed that outside military assistance was needed "to restore the constitutional order and to preserve the country's integrity", the government said in an appeal sent to the Western European Union (WEU).
In the Hague, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the EU presidency, said the EU was seriously considering the request.

But Kohl told reporters after talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok that the crisis was largely an internal affair and it was not clear what Western troops would do in Albania if sent there to help restore order.
In New York, Italy and Albania asked for an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council, urging the 15-member body to issue a statement before possible massacres break out.
A mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe led by former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky was due to leave from Vienna on Friday morning for Bari.
Helicopters would fly the 10-member delegation either to the Albanian mainland or an Italian ship for talks with political leaders and rebel representatives.
